Last month, we sent the Intendant general of Cuba, "Don Felipe Fernandez de Castro" to Haiti in a diplomatic mission to retrieve the eastern side of Hispaniola, which we lost 9 years ago. Sadly, the Haitian officials didn't seem to reason with us, arguing that our claim had lost legitimacy after the criollos overthrew the colonial government, but also even going as far as to say that our efforts to reestablish Spanish rule over the old empire was a "lost cause". De Castro left the island enraged and threatening the Haitian government with an invasion. It's now up to us whether to follow up on his words.

§RIf we can't even retake Santo Domingo, then there's no scenario in which we can reconquer the rest of the old empire§W

\n\nPresident Jean-Pierre Boyer addressed the Haitian people today with a proclamation about a recent meeting with representatives of Spanish Crown. As the meeting consisted of a Spanish request to the return Santo Domingo to Spain, a request which would be deeply unconstitutional to obligeâ€”the proclamation reassured the territorial integrity of the Republic. He reminded our people of our great union and reminded the people of the Eastern District that they joined Haiti willingly, urging them to remain at rest in our government that seeks only to bring them happiness and prosperity. In the end, Boyer's message is clearâ€”we will remain firmly committed to the territorial integrity of Haiti as a whole. Naturally, following his adress to the nation, Boyer took measures to East Haiti from its Spansish roots, persecuting symphatizers of Fernando VII and stripping the region of its Spanish symbols.

\n\nDue to the chaos of the Napoleonic Wars in Spain, many of its Colonies pursued greater autonomy or independence. In 1814, the restored Spanish king, Ferdinand VII, declared the developments in the Americas illegal and sent armies to quell the areas still in rebellion. The restoration was short lived, reversed by 1820 and Spain has lost almost all of its territories in the New World, but he has maintained hope in eventually recovering them. All his attempts prior to this point have been in vain, but the recent Reconquest of Santo Domingo has convinced many in the court that peharps the tide is turning in our favor. Even if the king doesn't live for much longer, we can continue expanding on his efforts to reestablish the old Empire, but we have to do it quick

\n\nIn January of 1830 the Kingdom of Spain sent a diplomatic mission with the intent of forcing us to cede over the eastern side of Hispaniola, and after our humble refusal they decided to scalate the dispute into an all-out war. Fortunately, we have managed to repeal any Spanish attempt at gaining a foothold in the island and they're now suing for peace, showing the world that no one can threathen our territorial integrity.

\n\nIn January of 1830 the Kingdom of Spain sent a diplomatic mission with the intent of forcing us to cede over the eastern side of Hispaniola, and after our humble refusal they decided to scalate the dispute into an all-out war. Unfortunately, They have not only managed to land near Santo Domingo but also to crush the bulk of our army in one military engagement, forcing us to sign a peace treaty where we renounce our rights to the Spanish Santo Domingo.

\n\nIt is still unclear to us wether it was our navy being in a deplorable state or our troops not having a good morale, but our attempts at succesfully invading Hispaniola have failed. With no many resources left for a new attempt, we had no other choice than to recognize Haitian rule over the whole island. A humiliation for what was once a great empire.

While the revolution has given liberals and progressives the opportunity to implement their reforms, it has also angered the traditionalist sectors for the very same reason. The Carlist pretender to the throne —Don Carlos VII, the Duke of Madrid— knew very well how to capitalize on this. After his party lost ground in the election of April 1872, amidst general allegations of fraud, his supporters retreated to the northwest and started insurrections in the rural areas of Aragon, Catalonia, and the Basque Country, the areas where Carlism tradicionally has found the most support. Thus, almost 40 years after the first war, Carlism emerges as an organized force yet again.

§RWar will start in 2 months§!

\n\nDespite the Carlist showing their most organized effort in years, their advance eventually came to a halt. Mainly because of their lack of siege equipment, which stopped them from capturing any of the major cities of the north. As time went on, our government gained stability, and as other threats to it disappeared we were able to allocate more resources into purging Carlist support in the North. Now almost all units loyal to Don Carlos have seized their activities, and the Carlist pretender ran away to France, waiting to see if he eventually gets another chance.

\n\nIt seems like Don Carlos couldn't have picked a better time for his rebellion. The infighting between Liberals, Progressives, and Democrats has not only hindered the response from the government in Madrid, but it has swayed the hearts of many people in favor of Carlism, which they now see as the only movement capable of restoring order in the country. After a swift siege, Carlos entered triumphant through the gates of Madrid, achieving a victory not even his father or grandfather could. Now the only thing he has to decide is the way he will rule.

The uprising at San Gil has made it clear that the strategy of the Liberal Union has failed: instead of integrating into the government, the Progressives are now on the run trying to overthrow Isabel. Yet despite this, O'Donnell is still going soft on them, refusing to carry out the Queen's order to execute all the prisoners from the uprising. She's now considering replacing him with Narvaez and his Moderate Party as leaders of the government.

§RKicking the Liberal Union out of the government could be catastrophic for the Bourbon Monarchy, but may lead to other faction rising up.§W

\n\nThis august the two main parties conspiring against the government, the Progressive party and the Democratic party, had their representatives meet far away from the government in the Belgian city of Ostend, where they signed a pact to cooperate in the overthrowing of the Bourbon monarchy. In the text they swore "To dismantle the monarchy and its political structure." and "To convene a constituent assembly, elected by universal suffrage through direct vote, to determine Spain’s government via national sovereignty." The vague wording of the first objective leaves the door open for other groups to sign in, in the hopes to attract more factions to their cause.

\n\nOnce in power again and in syntony with the Queen's wishes, Narvaez adopted a repressive policy that suspended constitutional guarantees and closed the Cortes. This however left the Liberal Union sidelined from the coalition government it had been a part of for more than a decade, fact that was made clear last December when Narvaez decided to have general Serrano and president of congress Antonio Ríos Rosas arrested for trying to open the Cortes again. Left with only a small representation in the senate after the most recent elections, the party has decided to withdraw from active political participation. They haven't agreed on anything with the liberal opposition yet, mainly because of O'Donnell's personal bitterness over the events at San Gil, but who knows if the situation changes in the near future

\n\nToday word has reached us that Leopoldo O'Donnell has passed away. Born into a noble family of Irish origin, the ex-prime minister was one of the most prominent defenders of the Queen's government. He sided with her in the Carlist war—even with most of his family flocking to the Carlist side—and was a loyal member of the army. After forming part in the revolution of 1854, him and other moderate liberals founded the Liberal Union in the unsuccesful attempt of integrating the progressives into his government. Suffering from Tifus, he retreated from politics and relocated to a summer house in Biarritz, France, where his life came to an end. His death opens the door to new leadership in the Liberal Union.

\n\nAfter O'Donnell's death a few months ago, we now recieve the news about the death of the most remarkable moderate leader, Ramón María Narváez. In the start of his career, Narvaez was a a loyal member of the army in the Liberal Triennium, and when absolutism was resoted briefly exiled to France, but coming back to service he rose through the ranks during the Carlist war. The regency of Espartero made him side with the moderates, and after the end of it he would become their main leader and one of the most prominent men in the government. General Luis González Bravo has replaced him as head of the moderates, but his death leaves a void amongst the leadership of the moderate party that maybe no man can fulfill.

After having made their preparations during their exile, opposition members of the Progressive traveled incognito to the port city of Cadiz, where they believed to be the place best suited for their ambitions. Just like they expected, on the 18th, general Prim revolted against the government of Her Majesty, and the revolution triumphed without bloodshed. In the early hours of the following day, the Provisional Revolutionary Junta was formed at the City Hall.
Despite this initial success, it seems like the revolutionaries did not plan very well the aftermath. The navy, still loyal to government in Madrid, started bombarding the main government facilities where the progressives were located. This in combination to their lack of supplies and low support from other towns in the Andalucian interior. It was only a matter of time before the Royal Army—headed by Manuel Pavia—came in and finished the rebels in a quick struggle. Prim, the leader of the rebellion, caught a bullet and died during the fight, and with him the progressive conspiration comes to an end.

After having made their preparations during their exile, progressives and democrats traveled incognito to the port city of Cadiz, where they believed to be the place best suited for their ambitions. Just like they expected, on the 18th, general Prim revolted against the government of Her Majesty, and the revolution triumphed without bloodshed. In the early hours of the following day, the Provisional Revolutionary Junta was formed at the City Hall.
The revolutionary movement spread like wildfire quickly through the rest of Andalucía, taking over the anger and frustration of the local people over unpopular measures such as the quintas or the censorship. However, without the navy on their side, the rebels couldn’t secure support along the coast or access key supplies they needed, and once the Royal Army came down we where able to win a smashing victory at the battle of Alcolea, where even Prim met his end. The immediate treat to the monarchy is over, but we now have to deal with all the unrest left by the whole situation.
